claim: TADs and many loops are formed by cohesin and positioned by CTCF.
source: TADs and many loops are formed by cohesin and positioned by CTCF.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about the roles of cohesin and CTCF in chromatin organization.

claim: In proliferating cells, cohesin mediates sister chromatid cohesion, which is essential for chromosome segregation.
source: In proliferating cells, cohesin also mediates sister chromatid cohesion, which is essential for chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cohesin's role in cell division.

claim: In G1-phase, there are ~250,000 nuclear cohesin complexes in HeLa cells.
source: In G1-phase, there are ~250,000 nuclear cohesin complexes, of which ~ 160,000 are chromatin-bound.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements using mass spectrometry and fluorescence-correlation spectroscopy as described in the manuscript.

claim: In G1-phase, ~160,000 cohesin complexes are chromatin-bound in HeLa cells.
source: In G1-phase, there are ~250,000 nuclear cohesin complexes, of which ~ 160,000 are chromatin-bound.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements combining FCS and FRAP data.

claim: Some genomic cohesin and CTCF enrichment sites are unoccupied in single cells at any one time.
source: Comparison with chromatin immunoprecipitation-sequencing data implies that some genomic cohesin and CTCF enrichment sites are unoccupied in single cells at any one time.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing absolute copy numbers with ChIP-seq data.

claim: Cohesin complexes are required for the formation of chromatin loops and TADs.
source: Cohesin complexes are not only required for the formation of chromatin loops and TADs (Gassler et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017), but also for sister chromatid cohesion, a prerequisite for chromosome segregation in mitosis and meiosis (reviewed in Morales and Losada, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cohesin is enriched at specific positions genome-wide, most of which are also associated with CTCF.
source: In interphase, cohesin is enriched at specific positions genome-wide, most of which are also associated with CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) (Parelho et al., 2008; Wendt et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CTCF consensus binding sites are frequently oriented convergently at TAD borders.
source: CTCF consensus binding sites are frequently oriented convergently at TAD borders (Rao et al., 2014; de Wit et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015) and depletion of CTCF leads to a reduction in insulation between TADs (Nora et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of CTCF leads to a reduction in insulation between TADs.
source: CTCF consensus binding sites are frequently oriented convergently at TAD borders (Rao et al., 2014; de Wit et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015) and depletion of CTCF leads to a reduction in insulation between TADs (Nora et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cohesin acts by extruding loops of DNA until it encounters convergently-oriented CTCF sites.
source: The mechanism by which cohesin and CTCF contribute to the generation of TADs is unknown, but it has been proposed that cohesin acts by extruding loops of DNA until it encounters convergently-oriented CTCF sites (Sanborn et al., 2015; Fudenberg et al., 2016), thus generating long-range interactions by tethering distal regions of the same chromosome together.
evidence: This is a proposed model cited from previous studies.

claim: Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex composed of four core subunits.
source: Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex composed of four core subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cohesin structure.

claim: The subunits SMC1, SMC3 and SCC1 form a tripartite ring structure.
source: The subunits SMC1, SMC3 and SCC1 (also called Rad21 or Mcd1) form a tripartite ring structure and associate via SCC1 with a fourth subunit, which exists in two isoforms in mammalian somatic cells termed STAG1 and STAG2 (also known as SA1 and SA2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cohesin structure.

claim: The fourth cohesin subunit exists in two isoforms in mammalian somatic cells termed STAG1 and STAG2.
source: The subunits SMC1, SMC3 and SCC1 (also called Rad21 or Mcd1) form a tripartite ring structure and associate via SCC1 with a fourth subunit, which exists in two isoforms in mammalian somatic cells termed STAG1 and STAG2 (also known as SA1 and SA2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cohesin composition.

claim: Recruitment of cohesin to chromatin in vivo depends on NIPBL and its binding partner MAU2.
source: Recruitment of cohesin to chromatin in vivo depends on NIPBL and its binding partner MAU2 (Ciosk et al., 2000; Gillespie and Hirano, 2004; Takahashi et al., 2004; Watrin et al., 2006; Schwarzer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NIPBL stimulates cohesin's ATPase activity in vitro.
source: NIPBL also stimulates cohesin's ATPase activity in vitro, an activity thought to be essential for loading of cohesin onto DNA (Arumugam et al., 2003; Weitzer et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2011; Ladurner et al., 2014; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014; Petela et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WAPL is required for cohesin's release from chromatin in interphase and prophase.
source: WAPL, on the other hand, is required for cohesin's release from chromatin in interphase and prophase, presumably via opening of the cohesin ring (Gandhi et al., 2006; Kueng et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012; Buheitel and Stemmann, 2013; Eichinger et al., 2013; Tedeschi et al., 2013; Huis in 't Veld et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Upon experimental depletion of WAPL in interphase cells, cohesin relocalises to axial elements termed vermicelli.
source: Upon experimental depletion of WAPL in interphase cells, cohesin relocalises to axial elements termed vermicelli (Tedeschi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Sororin is essential for maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in the presence of WAPL.
source: In S and G2 phase of the cell cycle, those cohesin complexes that mediate cohesion are protected from WAPL's releasing activity by the protein sororin, which is essential for maintaining sister chromatid cohesion (Rankin et al., 2005; Schmitz et al., 2007) in the presence of WAPL (Nishiyama et al., 2010; Ladurner et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromosome organisation is variable from cell to cell.
source: The few studies that used Hi-C to investigate the genome organisation of single cells have found that chromosome organisation is variable from cell to cell (Nagano et al., 2013; Flyamer et al., 2017; Gassler et al., 2017; Nagano et al., 2017; Stevens et al., 2017), raising the possibility that TADs might be the product of ongoing loop extrusion events that occur stochastically and are detectable only when averaging across a cell population.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous single-cell Hi-C studies.

claim: TADs might be the product of ongoing loop extrusion events that occur stochastically and are detectable only when averaging across a cell population.
source: The few studies that used Hi-C to investigate the genome organisation of single cells have found that chromosome organisation is variable from cell to cell (Nagano et al., 2013; Flyamer et al., 2017; Gassler et al., 2017; Nagano et al., 2017; Stevens et al., 2017), raising the possibility that TADs might be the product of ongoing loop extrusion events that occur stochastically and are detectable only when averaging across a cell population.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of single-cell Hi-C data.

claim: The cohesin subunits SMC3 and SCC1 were present in approximately 417,000 and 350,000 copies per G1 cell.
source: Using this approach, we found that the cohesin subunits SMC3 and SCC1 were present in approximately 417,000 and 350,000 copies per G1 cell (Figure 1, see Table 1 for exact values and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for individual peptide counts).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS quantification data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Between 61,000 and 69,000 copies of SMC1, SMC3 and SCC1 were detectable on chromatin in G1.
source: However, consistent with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry of these subunits on chromatin, between 61,000 and 69,000 copies of SMC1, SMC3 and SCC1 were detectable on chromatin in G1.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS quantification data.

claim: Around 15,000 copies of chromatin-bound STAG1 and 45,000 copies of STAG2 were detected in G1.
source: We detected around 15,000 copies of chromatin-bound STAG1 and 45,000 copies of STAG2 in G1, suggesting that cohesin-STAG2 is present in approximately three-fold excess over cohesin-STAG1 on chromatin in HeLa cells in G1; this ratio increased to 4.6-fold in G2 and decreased to 2.9-fold in prometaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS quantification data.

claim: Cohesin-STAG2 is present in approximately three-fold excess over cohesin-STAG1 on chromatin in HeLa cells in G1.
source: We detected around 15,000 copies of chromatin-bound STAG1 and 45,000 copies of STAG2 in G1, suggesting that cohesin-STAG2 is present in approximately three-fold excess over cohesin-STAG1 on chromatin in HeLa cells in G1; this ratio increased to 4.6-fold in G2 and decreased to 2.9-fold in prometaphase.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the measured copy numbers of STAG1 and STAG2.

claim: Between 60,000 and 70,000 cohesin complexes exist in chromatin fractions isolated by differential centrifugation from HeLa cells in G1 phase.
source: The combined total of STAG1 and STAG2 on chromatin was 60,000; taken together this suggests that, on average, between 60,000 and 70,000 cohesin complexes exist in chromatin fractions isolated by differential centrifugation from HeLa cells in G1 phase.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the measured copy numbers of cohesin subunits.

claim: The stoichiometry of cohesin remains close to 1:1:1:1 in G1, G2 and prometaphase.
source: Thus, the stoichiometry of cohesin remains close to 1:1:1:1 in G1, G2 and prometaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and LC-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The experiments are consistent with the monomeric ring model for cohesion establishment.
source: Since this is likely to be an underestimation of the true STAG1/2:SCC1 ratio, our experiments are consistent with the monomeric ring model for cohesion establishment.
evidence: This is an inference from the stoichiometry data.

claim: The G1 concentrations of SCC1 and STAG2 in the nucleus were measured to have a median of 330 nM and 280 nM, respectively.
source: The G1 concentrations of SCC1 and STAG2 in the nucleus were measured to have a median of 330 nM and 280 nM, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS measurements.

claim: The concentration of nuclear STAG1 was around 70 nM in G1.
source: Consistent with our LC-MS data, the concentration of nuclear STAG1 was lower, at around 70 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS measurements.

claim: Most cohesin complexes and cohesin regulators exist as monomers.
source: The counts per molecule (CPM) in all our EGFP-tagged cell lines was similar to that of mEGFP, indicating that most cohesin complexes and cohesin regulators exist as monomers (the mean of the median protein of interest: free mEGFP CPM ratios was 1 ± 0.3, Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from FCS measurements comparing CPM values.

claim: Approximately 260,000 copies of SCC1-mEGFP, 50,000 copies of STAG1-EGFP and 240,000 copies of STAG2-EGFP exist per G1 cell.
source: Using this approach, we estimated that approximately 260,000 copies of SCC1-mEGFP, 50,000 copies of STAG1-EGFP and 240,000 copies of STAG2-EGFP exist per G1 cell.
evidence: This claim is based on FCS measurements converted to absolute copy numbers.

claim: The two orthogonal methods (LC-MS and FCS) agree to within an average factor of 1.5.
source: Using bootstrapping, we estimated that the two orthogonal methods agree to within an average factor of 1.5, and that a ratio of one, that is equal protein numbers for the two methods, was within 68% of the error for 6 out of 9 conditions (Appendix 1—table 5, see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis comparing LC-MS and FCS data.

claim: The total copy number of cohesin subunits increased in G2 cells compared to G1 cells.
source: As also observed in the LC-MS dataset, the total copy number of cohesin subunits increased in G2 cells compared to G1 cells (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by both LC-MS and FCS data shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The intracellular concentration of cohesin was maintained in G2 despite the increase in total copy number, since the volume of G2 cells also increased.
source: The intracellular concentration of cohesin was maintained in G2 despite this increase in total copy number, since the volume of G2 cells also increased (Figure 2, Table 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This claim is inferred from FCS concentration measurements and cell volume measurements.

claim: NIPBL, WAPL, sororin and CTCF were all sub-stoichiometric relative to SCC1 in G1 and G2 HeLa cells.
source: We found that NIPBL, WAPL, sororin and CTCF were all sub-stoichiometric relative to SCC1 in G1 and G2 HeLa cells, although the 68% distribution intervals for nuclear SCC1 and NIPBL overlapped in G1 (Figure 2B and Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In G1 phase, cohesin is dynamically bound to chromatin with a residence time of 13.7 ± 2.2 min.
source: Consistent with previous studies that relied on ectopically expressed GFP-tagged cohesin subunits (Gerlich et al., 2006; Schmitz et al., 2007; Ladurner et al., 2014; Ladurner et al., 2016), the recovery kinetics obtained from G1 phase cells could largely be fitted using a single exponential function, indicating cohesin was dynamically bound to chromatin with a residence time of 13.7 ± 2.2 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by iFRAP measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In G2 phase, the recovery kinetics could only be fitted using a double exponential function with a dynamic residence time of 10.0 ± 3.1 min and a stable residence time of 8.6 ± 4.1 hr.
source: Also consistent with previous studies, the recovery kinetics obtained from cells in G2 phase could only be fitted using a double exponential function with a dynamic residence time of 10.0 ± 3.1 min and a stable residence time of 8.6 ± 4.1 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D,E and Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by iFRAP measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 64 ± 4% (160,000 ± 10,000) of nuclear SCC1-GFP molecules are bound to chromatin in G1.
source: According to our FCS analysis, approximately 250,000 copies of SCC1-GFP reside in the nucleus in G1. Our iFRAP analysis allowed us to estimate that approximately 64 ± 4% (160,000 ± 10,000) of these molecules are bound to chromatin (Figure 3C,D, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is based on combining FCS and iFRAP data.

claim: In G2, approximately 37 ± 9% of nuclear SCC1-EGFP is bound stably to chromatin, 36 ± 9% is bound dynamically and 27 ± 7% is soluble.
source: In G2, we estimate that 37 ± 9% of nuclear SCC1-EGFP is bound stably to chromatin, 36 ± 9% is bound dynamically and 27 ± 7% is soluble (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on iFRAP analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Around 108,000 ± 26,000 cohesin molecules are stably bound, 105,000 ± 26,000 bind dynamically and 79,000 ± 21,000 are soluble in G2 phase.
source: Taking into account our FCS measurements of SCC1-EGFP copy number in G2 phase, we estimate that around 108,000 ± 26,000 cohesin molecules are stably bound, 105,000 ± 26,000 bind dynamically and 79,000 ± 21,000 are soluble (Figure 3D, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is based on combining FCS and iFRAP data.

claim: The LC-MS and FCS estimates of the number of SCC1 molecules bound to chromatin in a HeLa cell agree to within a factor of 2.3 in G1 and a factor of 1.4 in G2.
source: Thus, our LC-MS and FCS estimates of the number of SCC1 molecules bound to chromatin in a HeLa cell agree to within a factor of 2.3 in G1 and a factor of 1.4 in G2 (Appendix 1—table 1, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is based on comparing LC-MS and FCS/iFRAP data.

claim: The number of chromatin-bound cohesin complexes increased by around a factor of two in G2 cells compared to G1 cells.
source: We observed that the number of chromatin-bound cohesin complexes increased by around a factor of two in G2 cells compared to G1 cells, as measured directly by LC-MS (Table 1) and indirectly by integrating our FCS and FRAP data (see above).
evidence: This claim is supported by both LC-MS and FCS/FRAP data.

claim: The only major distinction between cohesin dynamics in G1 and G2 phase cells is that a fraction of cohesin becomes stably bound in G2 phase.
source: Therefore, we propose that the only major distinction between cohesin dynamics in G1 and G2 phase cells is that a fraction of cohesin becomes stably bound in G2 phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mathematical modeling of the experimental data.

claim: Around 37,000, 35,000 and 47,000 sites for SMC3, STAG1 and STAG2, respectively, were identified in the mappable fraction of the human genome in G1-synchronised HeLa cells.
source: We have identified around 37,000, 35,000 and 47,000 sites for SMC3, STAG1 and STAG2, respectively in the mappable fraction of the human genome in G1-synchronised HeLa cells (Figure 5A, Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 88% of SMC3 sites overlap with the combined enrichment sites of STAG1 and STAG2.
source: 88% of SMC3 sites overlap with the combined enrichment sites of STAG1 and STAG2, and 77% overlap with CTCF (Figure 5B, Appendix 1—table 7.).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 77% of SMC3 sites overlap with CTCF.
source: 88% of SMC3 sites overlap with the combined enrichment sites of STAG1 and STAG2, and 77% overlap with CTCF (Figure 5B, Appendix 1—table 7.).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There should be around 117,000 cohesin enrichment sites per HeLa cell.
source: If we assume that cohesin occupies the HeLa genome (7.9 Mb; Landry et al., 2013) with equal frequency as in the 'mappable' human genome (2.7 Mb) there should be around 117,000 cohesin enrichment sites per HeLa cell (~40,000 ÷ 2.7 × 7.9).
evidence: This is an inference based on extrapolating ChIP-seq data to the full HeLa genome.

claim: Around 41,000 CTCF binding sites were identified in ChIP-seq experiments performed in G1-arrested HeLa cells.
source: We identified around 41,000 CTCF binding sites in ChIP-seq experiments performed in G1-arrested HeLa cells (Figure 5A, Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There are around 120,000 potential CTCF binding sites per HeLa cell.
source: Using the same logic as described above, this equates to around 120,000 potential CTCF binding sites per HeLa cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on extrapolating ChIP-seq data to the full HeLa genome.

claim: Approximately 180,000 copies of GFP-tagged CTCF reside in the nucleus in G1.
source: Using FCS, we estimated that approximately 180,000 copies of GFP-tagged CTCF reside in the nucleus in G1 (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by FCS measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: It is possible that not every CTCF site is occupied simultaneously by CTCF in a single G1 cell.
source: Given that we estimate that the number of CTCF molecules in the nucleus is similar to the number of CTCF binding sites, and assuming that at steady state not all CTCF molecules are chromatin bound, it is possible that not every site is occupied simultaneously by CTCF in a single G1 cell (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparing CTCF copy numbers with binding site numbers.

claim: Around 80% of the detected SMC3 enrichment sites resided within 100 kb of each other.
source: However, around 80% percent of the detected SMC3 enrichment sites resided within 100 kb of each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of SMC3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At least some cohesin complexes might extrude loops around 100 kb in size.
source: Nevertheless, this analysis suggests that at least some cohesin complexes might extrude loops around 100 kb in size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of cohesin enrichment sites.

claim: The LC-MS and FCS-derived estimates of total cohesin subunit copy number were within an overall factor of 1.3 of one another in G1 and 1.4 in G2.
source: As mentioned above, our LC-MS and FCS-derived estimates of total cohesin subunit copy number were within an overall factor of 1.3 of one another in G1 and 1.4 in G2 (Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This claim is based on comparing LC-MS and FCS data.

claim: FCS-derived estimates of chromatin-bound SCC1 were 2.3-fold higher than LC-MS estimates in G1 and 1.4-fold higher in G2.
source: Our FCS-derived estimates of chromatin-bound SCC1 were 2.3-fold higher than our LC-MS estimates in G1 and 1.4-fold higher in G2.
evidence: This claim is based on comparing LC-MS and FCS/iFRAP data.

claim: A fraction of dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin complexes was lost during the purification steps that preceded LC-MS analysis.
source: It is possible that a fraction of dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin complexes was lost during the purification steps that preceded our LC-MS analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between LC-MS and FCS/iFRAP measurements.

claim: If cohesin is mobile on chromatin, it is unlikely that every cohesin enrichment site is occupied in a single G1 cell.
source: If cohesin is indeed mobile on chromatin, our finding that the number of chromatin-bound cohesin complexes is similar to the number of potential cohesin binding sites means it is unlikely that every cohesin enrichment site is occupied in a single G1 cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing cohesin copy numbers with binding site numbers.

claim: If the chromatin-bound fraction of CTCF is below around 0.67, not all CTCF binding sites would be occupied simultaneously.
source: This suggests that if the chromatin-bound fraction of CTCF is below around 0.67, not all CTCF binding sites would be occupied simultaneously.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing CTCF copy numbers with binding site numbers.

claim: Only around 49% of nuclear CTCF molecules are chromatin-bound.
source: Importantly, these authors concluded that only around 49% of nuclear CTCF molecules are actually chromatin-bound (Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.

claim: To generate a 100 kb loop, a dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin complex would need to extrude at around 8 kb/min.
source: To generate a 100 kb loop (the genomic distance that covers more than 80% of cohesin enrichment sites; Figure 5C), a dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin complex would need to extrude at around 8 kb/min.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured residence time and estimated loop size.

claim: Using the median TAD size of ~185 kb, dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin would need to extrude at rates of around 14 kb/min.
source: Since we found that the distance between neighbouring cohesin enrichment sites was highly variable and cohesin occupancy at these sites is likely to be below 100%, an alternative estimate as to the dimensions of a typical chromatin loop is to use the median TAD size determined in Hi-C experiments (~185 kb, Rao et al., 2014). Using this value, dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin would need to extrude at rates of around 14 kb/min.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured residence time and median TAD size from a cited study.

claim: These calculated rates of dynamic cohesin-mediated loop extrusion are close to the predicted rate of loop extrusion by cohesin in HeLa cells (22.5 kb/min).
source: These calculated rates of dynamic cohesin-mediated loop extrusion are close to the predicted rate of loop extrusion by cohesin in HeLa cells (22.5 kb/min, Rao et al., 2017), condensin II in chicken cells (6–12 kb/min, Gibcus et al., 2018), SMC complexes in B. subtilis (54 kb/min, Wang et al., 2017) and the maximal rate of loop extrusion observed for yeast condensin in vitro (90 kb/min, Ganji et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim compares calculated rates with rates from cited studies.

claim: Cohesion is believed to be mediated by stably-bound complexes, which comprises around half of all chromatin-bound cohesin in G2.
source: Cohesion is believed to be mediated by stably-bound complexes, which comprises around half of all chromatin-bound cohesin in G2 (Figure 3C and Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on FRAP data and a cited study.

claim: Depletion of WAPL results in the stabilisation of cohesin complexes on chromatin and a dramatic change in chromatin architecture.
source: Depletion of WAPL results in the stabilisation of cohesin complexes on chromatin and a dramatic change in chromatin architecture, indicating that stably-bound cohesin complexes are able to function in chromosome organisation and that alteration of cohesin's residence time may influence this process (Kueng et al., 2006; Tedeschi et al., 2013; Gassler et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The number and position of TADs and loops does not differ significantly between G1 and G2 cells.
source: However, the number and position of TADs and loops does not differ significantly between G1 and G2 cells (Wutz et al., 2017), that is chromatin architecture does not detectably change even though many cohesin complexes are stably bound to chromatin in G2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The number of dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin complexes is actually reduced in G2 compared to G1.
source: However, even though the total number of cohesin complexes bound to chromatin in G2 is twice of that in G1, our FRAP data indicate that the number of dynamically chromatin-bound cohesin complexes is actually reduced (Tables 1, 2 and 3, and Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on FRAP data shown in Tables and Figures.

claim: Around 213,000 cohesin complexes are bound to chromatin in a typical G2 cell, of which around half are bound stably to chromatin.
source: Using FCS and iFRAP, we estimated that around 213,000 cohesin complexes are bound to chromatin in a typical G2 cell, of which around half are bound stably to chromatin (Table 3, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on FCS and iFRAP data shown in Table 3 and Figure 3D.

claim: Around 108,000 cohesin complexes establish cohesion between replicated genomes in G2.
source: Since the stable fraction is the one thought to mediate cohesion (Gerlich et al., 2006), this suggests that around 108,000 cohesin complexes establish cohesion between replicated genomes that each contain 117,000 predicted cohesin enrichment sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on FRAP data and cited knowledge.

claim: If cohesion is mediated by monomeric cohesin, it is unlikely that it is established at every cohesin enrichment site in a single cell.
source: Thus, if cohesion is mediated by monomeric cohesin, it is unlikely that it is established at every cohesin enrichment site in a single cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the number of cohesive cohesin complexes with the number of enrichment sites.

claim: Proximity to a cohesin enrichment site does not correlate with proximity between sister chromatids in G2.
source: This is consistent with the finding that proximity to a cohesin enrichment site does not correlate with proximity between sister chromatids in G2 (Stanyte et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Only around 14,000 cohesin complexes were bound to chromosomes in prometaphase-arrested HeLa cells.
source: Using LC-MS, we estimated that only around 14,000 cohesin complexes were bound to chromosomes in these cells (Figure 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Approximately 90% of all chromatin-bound cohesin complexes dissociate from chromosomes in prophase and prometaphase.
source: These numbers are in good agreement with the previous observation that approximately 90% of all chromatin-bound cohesin complexes dissociate from chromosomes in prophase and prometaphase (Waizenegger et al., 2000; Gerlich et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In prometaphase-arrested cells, cohesin is predominantly detected at centromeres.
source: Since previous immunofluorescence microscopy experiments have shown that in prometaphase-arrested cells cohesin is predominantly detected at centromeres (Giménez-Abián et al., 2004) and because ChIP experiments could not detect cohesin in the non-repetitive part of the genome in such cells (Wendt et al., 2008), we assume that most of the 14,000 cohesin complexes that we found on prometaphase chromosomes must have represented cohesin at centromeres.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited studies.

claim: Each HeLa chromosome might contain around 200 cohesin complexes in its centromeric region in prometaphase.
source: Since the HeLa cells used in this study contained on average 64 chromosomes (Landry et al., 2013), our measurements indicate that each of these chromosomes might contain around 200 cohesin complexes in its centromeric region.
evidence: This is an inference based on dividing total prometaphase cohesin by chromosome number.

claim: At least some but possibly many of the predicted cohesin enrichment sites are unoccupied in a single cell at a given timepoint.
source: Our findings suggest that at least some but possibly many of the predicted cohesin enrichment sites are unoccupied in a single cell at a given timepoint, implying that our current models of chromatin organisation and sister chromatid cohesion derived from large populations of cells may not fully reflect the situation in individual cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing copy numbers with enrichment sites.
